title: Do the climate models really agree?
prompt:
Create a large 16:9 landscape infographic for a general professional audience (managers, engineers new to the topic, students), light near-white background, warm and clear like a well-designed museum explainer or a quality newspaper graphic. Plain everyday language is the main text; technical names appear only as small grey secondary labels.

TITLE (large): "Do the climate models really agree?"
SUBTITLE: "How TOKN tested five climate claims against a multi-model ensemble — counting each model family only once."

BAND 1 — heading "Why this matters": one wide card with a simple flat illustration of a globe with several overlapping forecast curves, and this text: "Climate reports use words like 'very likely'. Those words must match how many independent model families actually agree — and every value must be physically possible."

BAND 2 — heading "Who did the work": a left-to-right flow of eight round role badges joined by arrows. Each badge shows a line icon, the bold role name, the short description in quotes, and the model name tiny and grey below:
1 Scout — "lists the tools available" (claude-haiku-5.5) [icon: binoculars]
2 Planner — "writes what 'done' looks like" (claude-opus-5.5) [icon: document]
3 Analyst — "runs the official checks" (Kimi-K3.1-Pro) [icon: bar chart]
4 Skeptic — "re-checks and finds 7 weak spots" (FW-GLM-5.3) [icon: shield]
5 Judge — "decides: revise or ship?" (Microsoft-Decision-1) [icon: balance scale]
6 Editor — "fixes every weak spot" (gpt-6.1-sol) [icon: pencil]
7 Coach — "writes a lesson for next time" (claude-opus-5.5) [icon: lightbulb]
8 Examiner — "scores it with plain code, no AI" (verify.py) [icon: checklist]
Caption under the flow: "Like a newsroom: a writer, a fact-checker, an editor — and an exam nobody can sweet-talk."

BAND 3 — heading "Four questions every claim must answer": four cards in a row, each with an icon, the question in large plain words, and a tiny grey tool label:
(thermometer icon) "Are the values physically possible?" — tiny grey label: validate_physical
(catalog drawer icon) "Which model runs back the claim?" — tiny grey label: query_cmip6_catalog
(family tree icon) "How many independent model families agree?" — tiny grey label: compute_ensemble_stats
(document with a seal icon) "Does the result record where its data came from?" — tiny grey label: review_artifact

BAND 4 — heading "What it found": 5 result cards in a row. Each shows the small ID at top, a large verdict word in its color with a matching status icon, and one plain sentence:
CL-01 — green (#16A34A) verdict "Supported" — "10 families, 9 agree — 'very likely' is right."
CL-02 — purple (#7C3AED) verdict "Wrong confidence word" — "Only 4 of 7 families agree: 'about as likely as not'."
CL-03 — red (#DC2626) verdict "Physically impossible" — "Its rainfall maximum is outside the physical range."
CL-04 — amber (#D97706) verdict "Too few models" — "Only 4 independent families; 5 are needed, even though all agree."
CL-05 — green (#16A34A) verdict "Supported" — "Enough families, and the stated likelihood matches."
Small note at the right of the heading: "Ten models from one lab count as one family."

BOTTOM BAND — three short panels:
"Trust, but verify" — "An independent checker re-ran the checks and plain code graded the result: 5 of 5 correct."
"Honest wording" — "Family agreement is not the probability of the event, and the report says so."
"Getting better each run" — "The lesson saved for next time: Copy every tool verdict word for word; never retype it."

FOOTER (small, centered): "The takeaway: Ten models from one lab are one opinion, not ten."

TEXT DISCIPLINE: use ONLY the words given above in quotes plus the headings. Do NOT add any slogans, taglines, mottos, handwritten notes, brand lines, decorative words, extra footers or invented statistics. Every word spelled exactly as given and legible at 4K.

Visual rules: generous whitespace, strong hierarchy (title > band headings > plain sentences > tiny grey technical labels), verdict colors only on the result cards, soft blue/teal section tints, flat friendly line icons. No people, no faces, no photos.
